case_study_insert.main_stem: Fleetline Fashion (FLF) is a public limited company in the value fashion retail sector, based in New York, employing a workforce of 90. Founded in 2016 by Renee Caldwell, it sells affordable clothing through 14 stores and a growing website, operating a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. FLF plans to invest $1,200,000 in a new automated distribution centre dedicated to its online own-label range, financed by an $800,000 share issue and a $400,000 bank loan. The business has fixed costs of $540,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.00 a unit and a selling price of $9.50, and currently produces 160,000 units a year. FLF faces rising unsold seasonal stock, now 18% of inventory, forcing deeper mark-downs.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Autumn/Winter 2026: Inspection rejected 3.1% of the 160,000 units (4,960 units), up from 2.4% last year. Unsold seasonal stock reached 18% of inventory value, and 24% of units were sold at discounted mark-down prices, up from 15% a year ago; the average mark-down was 35%. Fabric waste rose to 6.5% of cutting-room input, and 12% of purchase orders arrived late against an 11-week supplier lead time, driving over-ordering for the peak season.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Fleetline Fashion as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate to 6.25%, its highest level in a decade. (2) Cotton and synthetic fabric costs rose 14.0% year-on-year, squeezing value-fashion margins. (3) Consumer spending on clothing grew just 1.8%, well below inflation of 6.5%, with value retailers reporting falling footfall and heavier price reductions.

questions.question_text: FLF plans to fund the distribution centre with a share issue and a bank loan. Explain two advantages for FLF of using a share issue to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue raises the $800,000 with no interest charges and no fixed repayment schedule, which protects FLF at a time when its current ratio has already fallen from 2.01 to 1.78 and cash dropped from $85,000 to $45,000. Unlike the $400,000 bank loan, shareholders' capital cannot be called in on a set date, so FLF keeps maximum flexibility while the distribution centre ramps up.

Point 2: Issuing shares spreads the risk of a large, unproven $1,200,000 investment across many owners rather than concentrating it in debt. If the online own-label range underperforms, FLF owes shareholders no fixed interest — unlike a lender, they simply share in higher or lower returns. Financing two-thirds of the project with equity also preserves FLF's borrowing capacity for future trade finance or acquisitions, and avoids encumbering assets just as current liabilities have risen to $470,000.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to FLF's financing decision, liquidity trend and expansion.

questions.question_text: FLF is launching its online own-label range fulfilled from the new distribution centre. Consider national television advertising, short-video influencer marketing or billboard advertising in retail parks. Which should FLF choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: Television would publicise the own-label range to millions within weeks and give FLF instant national stature against larger rivals. However, production plus airtime would consume the $400,000 loan and far more, while much of the audience is not buying FLF at a $9.50 average price online, creating huge waste for a business already applying price reductions to 24% of its units.

Short-video influencer marketing: Short-video creators on the dominant social platforms can style, try on and price-compare the own-label range directly to price-sensitive younger shoppers, with spend tracked through views, clicks and redemption codes and fees flexible to performance. It matches FLF's margin structure, funnels traffic straight to the new website and distribution centre, and builds the kind of social proof that suits own-label discovery at low cost.

Billboard advertising in retail parks: Hoardings beside retail parks reach shoppers already in a buying mood and reinforce the own-label name locally. But static billboards are expensive, untargeted and impossible to segment by style or age, and they give no direct click-through to the website — a serious weakness when the objective is online penetration, not just store awareness.

Recommendation: FLF should choose short-video influencer marketing. It is the cheapest, most measurable and most precisely targeted way to put the own-label range in front of the exact online value shopper the new distribution centre exists to serve, and redemption data will show within weeks which creators drive orders. Television is rejected as unaffordable relative to returns at a $9.50 average selling price, billboards are rejected as unmeasurable and unable to drive tracked online orders, and the saved budget can scale influencer spend once results prove the channel.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the three promotional options with minimal application to FLF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of FLF with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of FLF with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and billboards are rejected.

questions.question_text: FLF's unsold seasonal stock has reached 18% of inventory. Explain two benefits for FLF of using democratic leadership to tackle this problem with its stores and buying team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership involves store managers and buying staff — who see daily what sells and what stagnates — directly in purchasing decisions, satisfying their esteem needs and tapping granular local knowledge of which sizes, colours and price points move in each of the 14 stores. Better-informed orders mean smaller commitments to slow lines, directly reducing the 18% unsold stock and the 24% of units now sold at an average 35% discount.

Point 2: Engaging the workforce builds commitment to markdown discipline: staff who help set clearance triggers and exit events take ownership of sell-through, flag emerging slow lines early and support the clearance strategy without demoralising the stores. Higher involvement raises motivation and reduces stock-count errors, helping managers trust the replenishment data feeding the new distribution centre and the 12% late purchase orders against the 11-week supplier lead time. Weekly huddles where staff review what moved and what did not keep everyone accountable for the sell-through rate the new centre depends on.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to FLF's overstock, markdowns and buying operation.

questions.question_text: FLF needs staff motivated to clear mark-down stock before the new distribution centre opens. Consider individual commission on full-price sales or a team-based bonus for hitting clearance targets. Which should FLF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Individual commission on full-price sales: A commission on each full-price unit sold pushes assistants to convert hesitant customers and upsell multiples, protecting contribution per unit and reducing reliance on mark-downs. However, commission distorts behaviour — staff may ignore the slow lines that hold 18% of inventory entirely, compete destructively against colleagues and neglect store housekeeping, which is the exact opposite of the clearance objective FLF faces with 24% of units already discounted.

Team-based bonus for clearance targets: A bonus paid to each store team when the branch clears its overstock targets aligns everyone — shop-floor, stockroom and layout teams — around one shared objective: moving aged seasonal stock. It encourages cross-colleague support, creative clearance displays and accurate stock counts, and spreads reward fairly across part-timers and full-timers. Its drawbacks are that free-riders may coast on others' effort and measuring one store's contribution is harder to attribute than individual till data.

Decision: FLF should choose the team-based clearance bonus. The problem is collective and urgent — 18% unsold stock, 24% of units marked down at an average 35% off, and deteriorating liquidity — and only a team incentive moves everybody in the same direction on the same lines simultaneously. Individual commission is rejected because it rewards selling what is easy rather than clearing what is stuck, widens gaps between colleagues and deepens the markdown spiral FLF is trying to escape ahead of the distribution centre opening.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of commission and team-based bonus with limited application to FLF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both motivation methods in the context of FLF.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in the context of FLF with a well-justified decision covering stock clearance, teamwork and behaviour.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how FLF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $540,000 ÷ ($9.50 − $5.00) = $540,000 ÷ $4.50 = 120,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 120,000 units a year.

Formula: Labour productivity = Output ÷ Number of employees. Substitution: 160,000 units ÷ 90 employees = 1,777.78 units per employee. Answer: labour productivity is 1,777.78 units per employee per year.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways FLF's management can use this break-even and productivity data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. FLF's managers can compare the 120,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 160,000 units, confirming a margin of safety of 40,000 units, and judge headroom for the new distribution centre before the full $1,200,000 is committed.
2. Labour productivity of 1,777.78 units per employee highlights which of the 14 stores under-perform; managers can redeploy or retrain staff and relieve picking queues feeding the online channel.
3. Contribution per unit of $4.50 underpins markdown strategy: at the current average 35% discount on 24% of units, managers can set clearance trigger prices store by store that still protect contribution above zero.
4. Unit cost data ($540,000 ÷ 160,000 units + $5.00 = $8.375, about $8.38) benchmarks performance every quarter, links the 3.1% of units failing inspection (4,960 units) to supplier quality, and quantifies the true cost of carrying 18% unsold stock into another season.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 120,000 units | (ii) Labour productivity = 1,777.78 units per employee | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 40,000 units against 160,000-unit output; productivity benchmarking across the 14 stores; markdown modelling at $4.50 contribution; unit-cost control at $8.375 a unit to cut the 3.1% inspection-failure rate and the 18% unsold stock.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate FLF's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has FLF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 2.01 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.78 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.91 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.67 : 1

Detailed workings: Current assets 2024 = $420,000 inventories + $260,000 trade receivables + $85,000 cash = $765,000. Current assets 2025 = $520,000 + $270,000 + $45,000 = $835,000. Short-term cover 2024 = $765,000 ÷ $380,000 = 2.01; 2025 = $835,000 ÷ $470,000 = 1.78. Stricter measure 2024 = ($765,000 − $420,000) ÷ $380,000 = $345,000 ÷ $380,000 = 0.91; 2025 = ($835,000 − $520,000) ÷ $470,000 = $315,000 ÷ $470,000 = 0.67.

Evaluation: Liquidity has deteriorated, not improved. Short-term cover fell from 2.01 to 1.78 because current liabilities rose from $380,000 to $470,000 while the growth in current assets came entirely from inventories swelling from $420,000 to $520,000 — unsold, discounted stock, not cash. The stricter measure fell from 0.91 to 0.67, meaning FLF now covers only two-thirds of short-term debts without selling inventory. Cash halved from $85,000 to $45,000 even as the $1,200,000 distribution centre commitment looms, and non-current assets jumped from $2,600,000 to $3,300,000, part-funded by the $400,000 bank loan and the share issue.

Conclusion: FLF's financial position has not improved. The deterioration in both measures — 2.01 to 1.78 and 0.91 to 0.67 — is driven by inventory build-up and rising liabilities rather than a stronger operating position. Before the distribution centre opens, FLF must clear the 18% unsold stock, tighten purchasing against the 11-week supplier lead time, cut the 35% average markdowns and rebuild cash through full-price conversion, or the new facility will push liquidity to uncomfortable levels.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether FLF's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for FLF of building a distribution centre dedicated to its online own-label range.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: A dedicated distribution centre lets FLF fulfil online own-label orders faster and cheaper, removing store-handling duplication and enabling next-day delivery at scale. It directly supports the own-label strategy — positioning stock smarter against the 11-week supplier lead time, reducing split shipments and feeding real-time sales data into automated replenishment — which protects margin on the $9.50 average price and accelerates clearance of the 18% unsold stock through targeted online promotions.

Disadvantage: The $1,200,000 investment, financed by an $800,000 share issue and a $400,000 bank loan, commits FLF to heavy fixed charges while its liquidity is already deteriorating — cash down to $45,000 and current liabilities up to $470,000. If online demand proves softer than planned, or the unsold stock fails to clear, the centre's fixed costs compound the markdown losses already visible (24% of units sold at an average 35% off), and the new borrowing adds interest at 6.25% to an already strained position.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to FLF's own-label plan, costs and liquidity trend.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 6.25%, the 14.0% increase in cotton and synthetic fabric costs and the 1.8% growth in clothing consumer spending will affect FLF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (to 6.25%): FLF's $400,000 bank loan would carry roughly an extra $25,000 a year of interest at the new rate, and future borrowing for the distribution centre will be pricier still. The rise also signals tighter monetary conditions, cooling discretionary clothing spend. Material but manageable, especially since FLF deliberately funded two-thirds of the project with the share issue to limit debt exposure.

Cotton and synthetic fabric costs (+14.0%): Goods are roughly $3.00 of FLF's $5.00 variable cost, so a 14.0% rise adds about $0.42 per unit — around $67,000 a year at 160,000 units. Unit contribution falls from $4.50 to about $4.08, break-even rises from 120,000 to roughly 132,000 units, and the margin of safety narrows from 40,000 to about 28,000 units. FLF must renegotiate fabric contracts, cut cutting-room waste below the current 6.5% and explore modest, surgical price rises rather than across-the-board increases.

Consumer spending on clothing grew just 1.8% against 6.5% inflation — a real-terms decline in demand. It strikes at FLF's weakest point: 18% unsold stock, 24% of units sold at an average 35% discount and a stricter liquidity measure that has fallen from 0.91 to 0.67. Weak demand means FLF cannot simply raise prices to recover fabric costs — it must keep price reductions to clear, eroding contribution further. It also undermines the sales case for the $1,200,000 distribution centre, whose economics assume growing online own-label volumes.

Conclusion: Weak consumer spending growth of 1.8% will have the greatest impact. Unlike the interest rise (bounded and largely pre-funded) or fabric inflation (about $67,000 a year, quantifiable and partly recoverable through pricing and waste reduction), falling real demand attacks FLF's revenue, its stock clearance and the viability of the distribution centre simultaneously — a compounding, revenue-side risk that should drive FLF's response: sharper buying against the 11-week lead time, aggressive full-price conversion of the 18% overstock, and phased investment milestones tied to measured online sales growth.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to FLF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on FLF's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of FLF with a well-justified judgment that weak consumer spending has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
